warmup.q: A service builds its issuer client lazily: if (client == null) { synchronized (Clients.class) { if (client == null) client = new GatewayClient(cfg); } } return client;. The client field is a plain static, and GatewayClient has some non-final fields. What can go wrong under load?
options: Nothing: the lock and the second check make it safe
A caller can get a non-null client whose non-final fields still hold their defaults
Two threads calling it at once deadlock
warmup.why: The lock and the second check do make sure only one client is built, so option 2 is wrong. The trouble is the first check: a thread that sees client != null never takes the lock, so nothing links its read to the constructor's writes. It can see the reference before the fields. Making the field volatile fixes it.

sections.h: Double-checked locking without volatile hands out half-built objects
sections.html:
Lazy initialization means building something on first use instead of at startup: a BIN table read from a 40 MB file, a connection to a card issuer, a signing key from a vault. The naive version is the check-then-act race from the first track:

Java
private static BinTable table;

static BinTable binTable() {
    if (table == null) {             // check
        table = new BinTable();      // act: two threads can both get here
    }
    return table;
}
Kotlin
private var table: BinTable? = null

fun binTable(): BinTable {
    if (table == null) {             // check
        table = BinTable()           // act: two threads can both get here
    }
    return table!!
}

It has two bugs. Two threads can both see null and both build a table, which wastes 50 ms, or opens two connections and leaks one. And it publishes the table through a plain field, so lesson 4 of this track applies: a reader can see the reference before the constructor's writes.

Marking the method synchronized fixes both. It's correct, and often good enough. But every caller now takes the lock on every call, forever, for a value that never changes after the first one. Under load, all request threads line up on one monitor just to read a field.

Double-checked locking (DCL) tries to skip the lock once the value exists:

Java
static BinTable binTable() {
    if (table == null) {                       // 1. first check, no lock
        synchronized (BinTable.class) {
            if (table == null) {               // 2. second check, under the lock
                table = new BinTable();
            }
        }
    }
    return table;                              // plain read on the fast path
}
Kotlin
private val lock = Any()

fun binTable(): BinTable {
    if (table == null) {                       // 1. first check, no lock
        synchronized(lock) {
            if (table == null) {               // 2. second check, under the lock
                table = BinTable()
            }
        }
    }
    return table!!                             // plain read on the fast path
}

The lock and the second check do stop two builds. The fast path is the problem. A thread that finds table != null never takes the lock, so it has no happens-before edge to the write inside it. The JIT and the CPU may let the reference out before the constructor's field writes. That thread can return a table that is not null and still empty.

The jcstress sample Singleton_07_BrokenNonVolatileDCL measured it. On AArch64, a singleton with a plain field came back non-null but without its data in about 1.8 million of 2.3 billion samples. When the singleton's field was final, it never failed, because final fields survive a race (lesson 4 of this track). That's why broken DCL often seems to work: many singletons happen to have only final fields, and x86 rarely shows the reordering. The simulator below lets you play the reordering yourself.

sim.title: Broken double-checked locking
sim.intro: T1 builds the table under the lock. Its two stores are listed in the order another thread may see them: the reference first, the fee second. T2 takes the lock-free fast path. Run T1 until it has published the reference, then switch. Can T2 charge with a fee of 0?

steps.code: table = t;   // the reference becomes visible first
t.fee = 120;   // the constructor's write, seen later
if (table != null) {   // fast path: no lock

goal.say: T2 charged with a fee of 0. It saw the reference but not the constructor's write, because its lock-free read has no edge to anything T1 did under the lock. A volatile table field forbids this order.

sections.h: Double-checked locking works when the field is volatile
sections.html:
Make the field volatile and DCL is correct. That has been true since Java 5, when JSR-133 gave volatile its release and acquire meaning. DCL's real job is a lazy field per instance; for a static, the holder idiom in the next section is simpler. So here is the instance version:

Java
class BinTableProvider {
    private volatile BinTable table;

    BinTable table() {
        BinTable t = table;                    // 1. fast path: one volatile read
        if (t != null) return t;
        synchronized (this) {                  // 2. slow path: one thread at a time
            t = table;                         // 3. check again: another thread may have won
            if (t == null) {
                t = new BinTable();
                table = t;                     // 4. volatile write publishes the finished table
            }
            return t;
        }
    }
}
Kotlin
class BinTableProvider {
    @Volatile private var table: BinTable? = null

    fun table(): BinTable {
        table?.let { return it }               // 1. fast path: one volatile read
        synchronized(this) {                   // 2. slow path: one thread at a time
            table?.let { return it }           // 3. check again: another thread may have won
            val t = BinTable()
            table = t                          // 4. volatile write publishes the finished table
            return t
        }
    }
}

The edge is the one from lesson 3 of this track. The volatile write in step 4 is a release, and the volatile read in step 1 is an acquire. A thread that reads a non-null table sees everything the building thread wrote before step 4, including every field the constructor set.

Three details matter.

Read the field once, into a local. A final return table would be a second volatile read. That's still correct, but the local keeps the fast path to one read. Joshua Bloch's Effective Java (item 83) writes it the same way.

Both checks matter. Drop the first and you've rebuilt the synchronized method. Drop the second and every thread that queued at the lock builds its own table, one after another. The Try it below shows that one.

Null needs care. DCL uses null to mean "not built yet", so an initializer that returns null runs again on every call. Kotlin's lazy uses a private sentinel instead, a marker object that only means "not built yet", and the jcstress sample Lazy_03_Basic keeps a separate volatile boolean.

If the initializer throws, nothing is stored, so the next caller tries again. Keep that in mind for the next section, because the holder idiom behaves differently.

try.title: Break DCL two ways
steps: Run DclDemo (Java or Kotlin) with the command below. Eight threads ask for a signing key at the same moment, and loading it takes 50 ms.
Delete the line marked try deleting this line. Predict the output, then run it.
Put the line back. Remove volatile (@Volatile in Kotlin). Predict, then run.

code.title: DclDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.jmm.l05; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.List; import java.util.Set; import java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentHashMap; import java.util.concurrent.CountDownLatch; import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger; /** Eight threads ask a hand-written double-checked lazy for the same value at the same moment. Edit it and rerun. */ public class DclDemo { static final class LazySigningKey { private volatile Object key; // try: remove volatile private final AtomicInteger loads; LazySigningKey(AtomicInteger loads) { this.loads = loads; } Object get() { Object k = key; // 1. fast path: one volatile read, no lock if (k != null) return k; synchronized (this) { // 2. slow path: one thread at a time k = key; // 3. check again: another thread may have won if (k != null) return k; // (try deleting this line) loads.incrementAndGet(); sleep(50); // fetching a signing key from a vault k = new Object(); key = k; // 4. volatile write publishes the key return k; } } } public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { for (int round = 1; round <= 3; round++) { AtomicInteger loads = new AtomicInteger(); LazySigningKey lazy = new LazySigningKey(loads); Set<Object> seen = ConcurrentHashMap.newKeySet(); CountDownLatch ready = new CountDownLatch(8), go = new CountDownLatch(1); List<Thread> threads = new ArrayList<>(); for (int i = 0; i < 8; i++) { Thread t = new Thread(() -> { ready.countDown(); try { go.await(); } catch (InterruptedException e) { return; } seen.add(lazy.get()); }); t.start(); threads.add(t); } ready.await(); go.countDown(); for (Thread t : threads) t.join(); System.out.printf("round %d: key loaded %d time(s), threads saw %d distinct key(s)%n", round, loads.get(), seen.size()); } } static void sleep(long ms) { try { Thread.sleep(ms); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } } }

Edit it and rerun. */ private class LazySigningKey(private val loads: AtomicInteger) { @Volatile private var key: Any? = null // try: remove @Volatile fun get(): Any { val k = key // 1. fast path: one volatile read, no lock if (k != null) return k synchronized(this) { // 2. slow path: one thread at a time val again = key // 3. check again: another thread may have won if (again != null) return again // (try deleting this line) loads.incrementAndGet() Thread.sleep(50) // fetching a signing key from a vault val fresh = Any() key = fresh // 4. volatile write publishes the key return fresh } } } fun main() { for (round in 1..3) { val loads = AtomicInteger() val lazy = LazySigningKey(loads) val seen = ConcurrentHashMap.newKeySet<Any>() val ready = CountDownLatch(8) val go = CountDownLatch(1) val threads = List(8) { thread { ready.countDown() go.await() seen += lazy.get() } } ready.await() go.countDown() threads.forEach { it.join() } println("round $round: key loaded ${loads.get()} time(s), threads saw ${seen.size} distinct key(s)") } }

try.expect: The correct version loads the key once per round, and all eight threads get the same key. Without the second check it loads 8 times and hands out 8 different keys: each thread that queued at the lock builds its own. Without volatile the output doesn't change at all. On an x86 laptop the missing edge almost never shows, so no run of this program can prove the code correct. That's the trap of broken DCL: you need a stress harness like jcstress, ideally on ARM, to see it fail.

sections.h: The holder class idiom lets the JVM do the locking
sections.html:
For a static singleton you don't need DCL at all. The JVM already has a lazy, thread-safe, run-once mechanism: class initialization.

The JLS (section 12.4) says a class is initialized right before its first active use: creating an instance, calling a static method, or reading a static field that isn't a compile-time constant. The JVM runs the static initializer once, under a per-class initialization lock, and every thread that uses the class afterwards sees what it wrote. That's the first safe publication idiom from lesson 4 of this track. The holder class idiom moves the instance into a nested class, so building it waits for the first call:

Java
public final class CardBinTable {
    private CardBinTable() { /* load 40 MB of BIN ranges */ }

    private static final class Holder {        // not initialized until instance() touches it
        static final CardBinTable INSTANCE = new CardBinTable();
    }

    public static CardBinTable instance() {
        return Holder.INSTANCE;                // first call initializes Holder, once, under the JVM's lock
    }
}
Kotlin
class CardBinTable private constructor() {
    private object Holder {                    // an object is initialized on first access
        val INSTANCE = CardBinTable()
    }

    companion object {
        fun instance(): CardBinTable = Holder.INSTANCE
    }
}

Your code has no volatile and no lock. The jcstress sample Singleton_09_Holder notes that in hot code the JIT will likely drop the initialization check, so instance() becomes a single field read.

It has three limits. It only works for statics: one instance per class, never one per bean or per tenant. The constructor can't take arguments you only know at runtime. And it never retries. If the initializer throws, the first caller gets ExceptionInInitializerError and every later caller gets NoClassDefFoundError: Could not initialize class CardBinTable$Holder, until the JVM restarts. A holder that connects to an issuer on first use turns one failed connection into a dead service.

An enum gives you the same guarantee: enum BinTable { INSTANCE; ... } is built by the enum's static initializer. Effective Java recommends it for singletons because serialization and reflection can't create a second instance. In Kotlin, an object declaration is the same idea; the docs say its initialization is thread-safe and done on first access.

One surprise: "lazy" here means on first use of the class, not of the instance. A plain static final INSTANCE in a class with other static methods is built the first time any of them runs. A Kotlin companion object is initialized together with its class. The holder exists to separate the two. The Try it shows exactly when each one is built.

try.title: When is each singleton built?
steps: Read HolderIdiomDemo. It has three singletons: an eager static final, a holder, and an enum (an object in Kotlin). Each one prints a line when it's built.
Before you run it, write down after which numbered step each built line will appear.
Run it, Java first, then Kotlin.

code.title: HolderIdiomDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.jmm.l05; /** When does each singleton get built? Watch the order of the lines. */ public class HolderIdiomDemo { // eager: built when the class is initialized, by the first use of anything static in it static final class EagerBins { static final EagerBins INSTANCE = new EagerBins(); private EagerBins() { System.out.println(" EagerBins built"); } static int tableSize() { return 3; } } // holder idiom: built when Holder is initialized, by the first call to instance() static final class LazyBins { private LazyBins() { System.out.println(" LazyBins built"); } private static final class Holder { static final LazyBins INSTANCE = new LazyBins(); } static LazyBins instance() { return Holder.INSTANCE; } static int tableSize() { return 3; } } // enum singleton: built when the enum class is initialized enum EnumBins { INSTANCE; EnumBins() { System.out.println(" EnumBins.INSTANCE built"); } static int tableSize() { return 3; } } public static void main(String[] args) { System.out.println("1. call EagerBins.tableSize()"); EagerBins.tableSize(); System.out.println("2. call LazyBins.tableSize()"); LazyBins.tableSize(); System.out.println("3. call LazyBins.instance()"); LazyBins.instance(); System.out.println("4. call LazyBins.instance() again"); LazyBins.instance(); System.out.println("5. call EnumBins.tableSize()"); EnumBins.tableSize(); } }

Watch the order of the lines. */ // eager: a companion object is initialized together with its class private class EagerBins private constructor() { init { println(" EagerBins built") } companion object { val INSTANCE = EagerBins() fun tableSize() = 3 } } // holder idiom in Kotlin: a private nested object is initialized on first access private class LazyBins private constructor() { init { println(" LazyBins built") } private object Holder { val INSTANCE = LazyBins() } companion object { fun instance(): LazyBins = Holder.INSTANCE fun tableSize() = 3 } } // Kotlin's own answer: an object declaration, built on first access and thread-safe private object BinTable { init { println(" BinTable built") } fun tableSize() = 3 } fun main() { println("1. call EagerBins.tableSize()") EagerBins.tableSize() println("2. call LazyBins.tableSize()") LazyBins.tableSize() println("3. call LazyBins.instance()") LazyBins.instance() println("4. call LazyBins.instance() again") LazyBins.instance() println("5. call BinTable.tableSize()") BinTable.tableSize() }

try.expect: EagerBins built appears right after step 1: calling a static method initialized the class, which built INSTANCE. LazyBins built appears only after step 3, the first instance() call, because tableSize() in step 2 never touched Holder, and it doesn't appear again in step 4. The enum (or Kotlin object) is built in step 5, the first time anything in it runs. Class initialization is lazy per class; the holder makes it lazy per instance.

sections.h: Kotlin's by lazy is double-checked locking, in three modes
sections.html:
val x by lazy { ... } is the DCL from earlier, written once in the standard library. The property compiles to a private final kotlin.Lazy x$delegate field, and the getter calls its getValue(). The default mode is LazyThreadSafetyMode.SYNCHRONIZED. Its implementation class, SynchronizedLazyImpl, has a volatile value field, a fast path that reads it once, and a synchronized block with a second check. It adds three things to the hand-written version: a sentinel instead of null, so a null result is cached too; a retry, because the docs promise that an initializer that throws runs again on the next access; and it drops the initializer after the first run, so whatever the lambda captured can be collected.

Java
// Java has no by lazy: a DCL field stands in for SYNCHRONIZED, a compareAndSet for PUBLICATION
final class IssuerGateway {
    private final Vault vault;
    private volatile SigningKey signingKey;
    private final AtomicReference<Map<String, String>> routes = new AtomicReference<>();

    IssuerGateway(Vault vault) { this.vault = vault; }

    SigningKey signingKey() {
        SigningKey k = signingKey;
        if (k != null) return k;
        synchronized (this) {
            if (signingKey == null) signingKey = vault.fetch("issuer-signing-key");
            return signingKey;
        }
    }

    Map<String, String> routes() {
        Map<String, String> r = routes.get();
        if (r != null) return r;
        routes.compareAndSet(null, parseRoutes(ROUTES_JSON));   // losers throw their result away
        return routes.get();
    }
}
Kotlin
class IssuerGateway(private val vault: Vault) {
    val signingKey: SigningKey by lazy {                    // SYNCHRONIZED: runs once, others wait
        vault.fetch("issuer-signing-key")
    }
    val routes: Map<String, String> by lazy(LazyThreadSafetyMode.PUBLICATION) {
        parseRoutes(ROUTES_JSON)                            // may run more than once; one result wins
    }
}
Mode The initializer runs Use it for
SYNCHRONIZED (default) once; other callers wait on a lock anything expensive or with side effects
PUBLICATION maybe on several threads at once; one result wins cheap, side-effect-free work
NONE with no synchronization at all values that never leave one thread

Keep the default unless you have a reason. PUBLICATION fits a cheap, pure initializer when you'd rather waste a little work than block. The losers' results are thrown away without cleanup, so never use it for something that opens a connection. NONE fits single-threaded hot code. Never put it on a property of a shared bean or singleton: the docs call the multi-threaded behavior unspecified, and the demo below shows eight threads getting eight different values.

SYNCHRONIZED has two traps. The lock is held while the initializer runs, so a 120 ms issuer call inside lazy makes every concurrent caller wait 120 ms. And by default the lock is the Lazy object itself; the docs warn that synchronizing on it from your own code can deadlock.

try.title: Race the three lazy modes
steps: For each mode, predict how many times the 50 ms initializer runs and how many distinct values eight threads see.
Run the Kotlin demo with the command below, then the Java twin, which builds the three modes by hand.
Change the sleep from 50 to 0 and run it a few times. Which numbers move?

code.title: LazyModesDemo.kt
code.html: package workbench.jmm.l05 import java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentHashMap import java.util.concurrent.CountDownLatch import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger import kotlin.concurrent.thread /** Eight threads read the same lazy value at the same moment, once for each LazyThreadSafetyMode. */ fun main() { for (mode in LazyThreadSafetyMode.entries) { val runs = AtomicInteger() val signingKey: Lazy<Any> = lazy(mode) { runs.incrementAndGet() Thread.sleep(50) // a slow initializer, like fetching a key from a vault Any() } val seen = ConcurrentHashMap.newKeySet<Any>() val go = CountDownLatch(1) val threads = List(8) { thread { go.await() seen += signingKey.value } } go.countDown() threads.forEach { it.join() } println("%-12s initializer ran %d time(s), threads saw %d distinct value(s)".format(mode, runs.get(), seen.size)) } }

These are the closest Java equivalents of Kotlin's three LazyThreadSafetyMode values. /** Eight threads read the same lazy value at the same moment, once for each kind of lazy. */ public class LazyModesDemoJava { // like SYNCHRONIZED: double-checked locking, so the initializer runs once static Supplier<Object> synchronizedLazy(Supplier<Object> init) { return new Supplier<>() { private volatile Object value; @Override public Object get() { Object v = value; if (v != null) return v; synchronized (this) { if (value == null) value = init.get(); return value; } } }; } // like PUBLICATION: any thread may compute, and the first compareAndSet wins static Supplier<Object> publicationLazy(Supplier<Object> init) { AtomicReference<Object> ref = new AtomicReference<>(); return () -> { Object v = ref.get(); if (v != null) return v; ref.compareAndSet(null, init.get()); return ref.get(); }; } // like NONE: no synchronization at all, only safe on one thread static Supplier<Object> unsafeLazy(Supplier<Object> init) { Object[] box = new Object[1]; return () -> { if (box[0] == null) box[0] = init.get(); return box[0]; }; } public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { race("SYNCHRONIZED", LazyModesDemoJava::synchronizedLazy); race("PUBLICATION", LazyModesDemoJava::publicationLazy); race("NONE", LazyModesDemoJava::unsafeLazy); } interface LazyFactory { Supplier<Object> make(Supplier<Object> init); } static void race(String name, LazyFactory factory) throws InterruptedException { AtomicInteger runs = new AtomicInteger(); Supplier<Object> signingKey = factory.make(() -> { runs.incrementAndGet(); sleep(50); // a slow initializer, like fetching a key from a vault return new Object(); }); Set<Object> seen = ConcurrentHashMap.newKeySet(); CountDownLatch go = new CountDownLatch(1); List<Thread> threads = new ArrayList<>(); for (int i = 0; i < 8; i++) { Thread t = new Thread(() -> { try { go.await(); } catch (InterruptedException e) { return; } seen.add(signingKey.get()); }); t.start(); threads.add(t); } go.countDown(); for (Thread t : threads) t.join(); System.out.printf("%-12s initializer ran %d time(s), threads saw %d distinct value(s)%n", name, runs.get(), seen.size()); } static void sleep(long ms) { try { Thread.sleep(ms); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } } }

try.expect: SYNCHRONIZED: 1 run, 1 value. PUBLICATION: up to 8 runs (here all 8, because every thread started before the first finished) but 1 value, because the first compareAndSet won and everyone returns its result. NONE: 8 runs and 8 values, each thread keeping its own. With no sleep, PUBLICATION and NONE usually run fewer times, because some threads arrive after the first one finished. The bug in NONE didn't go away. The window got smaller.

analogy: Lazy init is the first person into the office making coffee. With no rule, three people arrive at once, see an empty pot, and brew three pots. A rule that everyone checks in at reception before touching the pot works, but then everyone queues at reception for every cup, all day. Double-checked locking says: look at the pot; if it's full, pour; if it's empty, go to reception, look again, and brew. It only works if the pot is see-through, which is what volatile gives you: you never pour from a pot that looks full but is still brewing. That's where the analogy breaks. In an office you can see the coffee brewing. In the JVM, without volatile, a half-built object looks exactly like a finished one.
world: Lazy fields hide in every Quarkus service: an issuer client built on the first request, a BIN table, a JWT signing key fetched from a vault, a Kafka producer created when the first message goes out. CDI already makes @ApplicationScoped beans lazy: the container creates the instance once, on the first call through its proxy, so the bean itself is safe. Look instead at lazy state inside a bean, a field filled in by a getter. In Kotlin use by lazy; in Java use a volatile DCL field. Better still, if every payment needs the value, load it at startup with @Startup or a StartupEvent observer, so a failure shows at deploy time instead of on the first authorization. And keep holders away from anything that can fail, such as a Temporal activity's client: after one failed initialization, every retry of the activity on that worker fails with NoClassDefFoundError until the worker restarts.
mistake: The most common mistake is leaving volatile off double-checked locking, because the code obviously builds only one instance. It does build only one. The bug is on the fast path, which reads the field with no edge to the write, and it almost never shows on x86 test machines, so it survives years of green builds and then fails on ARM. The fix is one word: volatile on the field (@Volatile in Kotlin). Better still, don't hand-write DCL. Use the holder idiom for statics, by lazy in Kotlin, and computeIfAbsent for one value per key.

compare.title: One lazy value per key: computeIfAbsent in Java, and the getOrPut trap in Kotlin

java.title: IssuerClients.java
java.html: class IssuerClients { private final ConcurrentMap<String, IssuerClient> clients = new ConcurrentHashMap<>(); IssuerClient clientFor(String issuerId) { // connect runs at most once per absent key; other callers for that key wait for it return clients.computeIfAbsent(issuerId, this::connect); } private IssuerClient connect(String issuerId) { return new IssuerClient(issuerId); // opens a connection } }

kotlin.title: IssuerClients.kt
kotlin.html: class IssuerClients { private val clients = ConcurrentHashMap<String, IssuerClient>() // looks the same, isn't: two threads can both run connect() for one key fun clientForRacy(issuerId: String): IssuerClient = clients.getOrPut(issuerId) { connect(issuerId) } // the same guarantee as Java: call the JDK method fun clientFor(issuerId: String): IssuerClient = clients.computeIfAbsent(issuerId) { connect(it) } private fun connect(issuerId: String): IssuerClient = IssuerClient(issuerId) // opens a connection }

compare.note: Kotlin's getOrPut on a ConcurrentMap never replaces a value that is already there, but its docs say the lambda may run even if the key is already in the map. Two threads can both connect, every caller ends up with the same client, and the losing connection is dropped without being closed. computeIfAbsent is the JDK's atomic version: the function runs at most once per absent key. Its Javadoc asks you to keep that function short, because other updates to the map can block while it runs. For a slow connect, store a lazy in the map, clients.computeIfAbsent(id) { lazy { connect(id) } }.value, so the map is busy only while the cheap Lazy object is created.

worked.title: Make a lazily loaded fraud-rules field safe

steps.say: A rules provider downloads fraud rules on first use. At startup a burst of 200 authorizations arrives at once. Name the two bugs, then choose an idiom before you read on.
steps.code: @ApplicationScoped public class FraudRulesProvider { @Inject RulesClient rulesClient; private FraudRules rules; // plain field public FraudRules rules() { // called by every request thread if (rules == null) { rules = rulesClient.download(); // 300 ms, and it can fail } return rules; } }

alt.html: @ApplicationScoped class FraudRulesProvider(private val rulesClient: RulesClient) { private var rules: FraudRules? = null // plain field fun rules(): FraudRules { // called by every request thread if (rules == null) { rules = rulesClient.download() // 300 ms, and it can fail } return rules!! } }

steps.say: First, check-then-act: every request in the first 300 ms sees null and starts its own download. Second, a plain field: a request thread can see the reference before the rules' fields. Now the idiom. Not the holder: the field belongs to a bean, and a failed download must be retried on the next request, not turned into NoClassDefFoundError. A volatile DCL field fits, and in Kotlin by lazy is that DCL.
Write it with subgoal labels. In Kotlin the whole thing is one line, and the retry on failure comes from the standard library.
steps.code: @ApplicationScoped public class FraudRulesProvider { @Inject RulesClient rulesClient; private volatile FraudRules rules; // 1. volatile: the fast path needs the edge public FraudRules rules() { FraudRules r = rules; // 2. fast path: one volatile read if (r != null) return r; synchronized (this) { // 3. slow path: one download at a time r = rules; if (r == null) { // 4. check again: someone may have won r = rulesClient.download(); // if this throws, nothing is stored rules = r; // 5. publish the finished rules } return r; } } }

alt.html: @ApplicationScoped class FraudRulesProvider(private val rulesClient: RulesClient) { // SYNCHRONIZED by default: steps 1 to 5 of the Java version, plus a retry if download() throws val rules: FraudRules by lazy { rulesClient.download() } }

steps.say: Ask one more question: does every authorization need the rules anyway? Then lazy buys you a slow first request and a failure you find on the first payment instead of at deploy. Load the rules at startup and publish them through a volatile field, as in lesson 4 of this track. Keep lazy for values that some requests never need.

lab.title: Three lazy initializers that build exactly once
steps: Run the tests once. All six fail: the DoubleCheckedLazy tests hit the TODO or find no volatile field, the stub builds eight BIN tables, and it connects to one issuer eight times.

Write DoubleCheckedLazy: a volatile field for the value, a field for the initializer, a fast path with one volatile read, and a synchronized slow path that checks again. Set the initializer to null once it has run.
Rewrite CardBinTable.instance() with the holder class idiom. Keep creations() as it is: calling it must not build the table.
Fix IssuerClients.clientFor with one map call, so each issuer is connected exactly once.
Run the tests until all six pass, then twice more.
hints: The initializer field is only read and written inside the lock, so it doesn't need to be volatile. The value field is read outside the lock, so it does.

In CardBinTable, delete the static instance field and add private static final class Holder { static final CardBinTable INSTANCE = new CardBinTable(); }. Ask yourself why calling creations() doesn't initialize Holder.
ConcurrentHashMap.computeIfAbsent runs the function at most once per absent key. The compare block shows why Kotlin's getOrPut would not be enough.
lab.done: All six tests in LazyInitTest pass, three runs in a row.

drill.title: Holder and volatile DCL from memory
drill.prompt: Close this page. Write (1) a static BinTable.instance() with the holder class idiom, and (2) a per-instance signingKey() with double-checked locking. Mark the line that needs volatile and say why. Then compare with the answer. Did you read the volatile field only once on the fast path?

answer.html: public final class BinTable { private BinTable() { /* load the table */ } private static final class Holder { static final BinTable INSTANCE = new BinTable(); // built once, under the class-init lock } public static BinTable instance() { return Holder.INSTANCE; } } public final class IssuerGateway { private final Vault vault; private volatile SigningKey key; // volatile: the fast path reads it without the lock public IssuerGateway(Vault vault) { this.vault = vault; } public SigningKey signingKey() { SigningKey k = key; // one volatile read if (k != null) return k; synchronized (this) { k = key; // check again under the lock if (k == null) { k = vault.fetch("issuer-signing-key"); key = k; // volatile write publishes the finished key } return k; } } }

alt.html: class BinTable private constructor() { private object Holder { val INSTANCE = BinTable() // built once, on first access to Holder } companion object { fun instance(): BinTable = Holder.INSTANCE } } class IssuerGateway(private val vault: Vault) { @Volatile private var key: SigningKey? = null // the fast path reads it without the lock fun signingKey(): SigningKey { key?.let { return it } // one volatile read synchronized(this) { key?.let { return it } // check again under the lock val k = vault.fetch("issuer-signing-key") key = k // volatile write publishes the finished key return k } } // in real Kotlin code: val signingKey by lazy { vault.fetch("issuer-signing-key") } }

recap: Naive lazy init is check-then-act on a plain field: it can build twice and publish a half-built object.
Double-checked locking without volatile builds once but is still broken: the lock-free fast path has no edge to the write.
With a volatile field, DCL is correct. Read the field once into a local, keep both checks, and use a sentinel if the value can be null.
The holder class idiom rides on class initialization: lazy, locked by the JVM, free after the first call, but static only and it never retries after a failure.
Kotlin's by lazy is a volatile DCL with a null-safe sentinel and retry on failure. PUBLICATION may run the initializer several times; NONE is for one thread only.
Prefer no laziness at all: if every request needs the value, load it at startup.

explain.prompt: A teammate asks: "In our double-checked locking, the write to table happens inside a synchronized block. Why does the field still need to be volatile?" Explain it in your own words.
explain.answer: The synchronized block only gives an edge to threads that take the same lock. The whole point of DCL is that the fast path doesn't take the lock: once table is set, callers read it and return. That read has no edge to the write, so the JIT and CPU are free to let the reference become visible before the constructor's writes, and a caller can get a table that isn't null but isn't built either. Making the field volatile turns the write into a release and the fast-path read into an acquire, so a thread that sees the reference also sees everything written before it. The lock is still needed, for a different job: making sure only one thread builds the table.

deeper.html:
A lazy object can itself be published through a race, and then its own fields matter. Kotlin's SynchronizedLazyImpl has a non-final initializer field, because it sets it to null after the first run. The jcstress sample Lazy_01_BrokenFactory shows what a non-final factory field costs. On AArch64, when the lazy object itself reached another thread through a plain field, that thread sometimes saw the factory as null and failed, and in one sample the factory ran twice. by lazy doesn't hit this in practice, because the compiler keeps the Lazy in a private final x$delegate field, and final fields are safe once the owner's constructor has finished. If you write your own lazy wrapper and also want to drop the initializer, Lazy_05_WrapperOneShot shows the fix: a final field pointing to a small wrapper that holds the factory.

Class initialization has one more rule worth knowing. Reading a static final field that is a compile-time constant, such as static final int MAX_BINS = 3, does not initialize the class at all: javac copies the value into the caller. That's why a holder only triggers on fields like INSTANCE, whose value is computed at runtime.

The JDK is growing its own answer. JDK 25 previewed stable values (JEP 502). JDK 26 renamed the idea lazy constants (JEP 526, second preview), and JDK 27 has a third preview (JEP 531). It is a JDK type for a value that is computed at most once and that the JIT may then treat as a constant, which a volatile field can never be. It is a preview API, so it needs --enable-preview and stays out of these labs, but it is worth following if you write libraries.

Finally, the history. "The Double-Checked Locking is Broken" declaration, signed by memory model researchers and JVM engineers before Java 5, explains why no clever trick could save DCL under the old memory model. The JSR-133 memory model of Java 5 fixed it by giving volatile its acquire and release meaning, which is the fix you used today.
